Why I Ditched Entity Framework for Raw SQL in .NET 10 — and Doubled My Fintech App’s Speed

The Controversial Decision That Paid Off

Why I Ditched Entity Framework for Raw SQL in .NET 10 — and Doubled My Fintech App’s Speed

The Controversial Decision That Paid Off

I used to love Entity Framework — until my fintech app’s trade history endpoint hit 100ms under load. I ripped it out, went raw SQL on .NET 10, and slashed it to 50ms. Controversial? Maybe. Worth it? Hell yes.

As a senior developer with 8+ years in the fintech space, I’ve built everything from payment processing systems to trading platforms. I’m not an ORM hater — Entity Framework has been my trusted companion for years. But when milliseconds translate directly to money and user satisfaction, sometimes you need to make tough architectural decisions.

This isn’t about bashing ORMs — it’s about knowing when to use the right tool for specific performance requirements. By the end of this article, you’ll understand exactly when and how to make this transition, complete with code examples, performance metrics, and a decision framework you can apply to your own projects.

Where Entity Framework Falls Short

Entity Framework Core has rightfully earned its place as the go-to data access solution in the .NET ecosystem. Its ability to abstract away database interactions and provide a clean, object-oriented interface is undeniably powerful. For many applications — perhaps even most — it’s the perfect solution.

But in the high-stakes world of fintech, we encountered several pain points:

Query Complexity and Performance

Our trading platform processes millions of transactions daily, with complex queries joining across multiple tables. As our application grew, certain queries became increasingly complex, with Entity Framework generating SQL that wasn’t always optimal:

  • Excessive JOINs when simpler approaches would suffice
  • Suboptimal filtering that happened in memory rather than at the database level
  • Inefficient translations of LINQ expressions to SQL

Memory Overhead

During peak trading hours, our system would handle thousands of concurrent users, each potentially executing multiple database operations. Under this load, we observed:

  • High memory allocation from tracking entities we didn’t need to track
  • Significant GC pressure affecting overall application performance
  • Degraded response times as connection pools saturated

The N+1 Query Problem

Despite our best efforts to use Include() and eager loading appropriately, we still occasionally hit the dreaded N+1 query pattern, where retrieving a collection triggered additional queries for each item.

Before optimization, our trade history endpoint — a critical feature for our users — took an average of 98ms to respond under typical load. During market volatility events, this would spike to 150ms or higher. For traders making split-second decisions, this was unacceptable.

How .NET 10 Changed the Game

When .NET 10 Preview 1 dropped on March 3, 2025, I immediately started testing our application against it. The performance improvements were impressive across the board, but what caught my attention was how much faster the base ADO.NET components had become.

Several key improvements in .NET 10 made raw SQL more attractive:

  • Improved SqlClient Performance: The foundational data access components saw significant optimizations, reducing overhead for raw SQL operations.
  • Enhanced Memory Management: Better handling of large result sets and reduced allocations for string operations — critical for SQL queries.
  • Faster Type Conversion: Improvements in converting between SQL types and .NET types reduced serialization/deserialization costs.
  • Native AOT Support: Better compatibility with trimming and Native AOT compilation for data access code.

These improvements meant that the performance gap between EF Core and raw SQL was now even more pronounced. The “convenience tax” of using an ORM had effectively increased.

The Migration: Process and Challenges

I didn’t rip out Entity Framework overnight. Instead, I took a methodical approach:

  1. Profiling and Identifying Bottlenecks: Using Application Insights and SQL Server Profiler, I identified our ten most expensive queries.
  2. Benchmarking: For each candidate query, I created benchmark tests comparing the EF implementation against a raw SQL equivalent.
  3. Incremental Migration: Starting with the highest-impact queries, I gradually replaced EF with optimized raw SQL.

The first challenge was convincing my team. Many were initially resistant — concerns about SQL injection, code maintainability, and losing the benefits of the ORM were raised. To address these, I created a mini-framework that maintained safety while delivering performance.

Another significant challenge was maintaining the domain model mapping. Entity Framework handles this automatically, but with raw SQL, we needed a solution. We settled on using Dapper for this purpose — it provided a lightweight way to map results to our domain objects without the overhead of a full ORM.

Code Comparison: Before and After

Let’s look at one of our most problematic endpoints — fetching a paginated trade history with filtering options:

Before: Entity Framework Implementation

public async Task<PagedResult<TradeDto>> GetTradeHistoryAsync(
    int accountId, 
    DateTime startDate, 
    DateTime endDate, 
    string assetClass = null, 
    int page = 1, 
    int pageSize = 20)
{
    var query = _context.Trades
        .Include(t => t.Instrument)
        .Include(t => t.ExecutionVenue)
        .Where(t => t.AccountId == accountId)
        .Where(t => t.TradeDate >= startDate && t.TradeDate <= endDate);
        
    if (!string.IsNullOrEmpty(assetClass))
    {
        query = query.Where(t => t.Instrument.AssetClass == assetClass);
    }
    
    var totalItems = await query.CountAsync();
    
    var trades = await query
        .OrderByDescending(t => t.TradeDate)
        .Skip((page - 1) * pageSize)
        .Take(pageSize)
        .Select(t => new TradeDto
        {
            TradeId = t.TradeId,
            InstrumentName = t.Instrument.Name,
            Quantity = t.Quantity,
            Price = t.Price,
            TradeDate = t.TradeDate,
            ExecutionVenue = t.ExecutionVenue.Name,
            AssetClass = t.Instrument.AssetClass,
            Direction = t.Direction,
            NotionalValue = t.Quantity * t.Price * t.Instrument.ContractMultiplier
        })
        .ToListAsync();
    
    return new PagedResult<TradeDto>
    {
        Items = trades,
        TotalItems = totalItems,
        Page = page,
        PageSize = pageSize
    };
}

After: Raw SQL Implementation

public async Task<PagedResult<TradeDto>> GetTradeHistoryAsync(
    int accountId, 
    DateTime startDate, 
    DateTime endDate, 
    string assetClass = null, 
    int page = 1, 
    int pageSize = 20)
{
    var parameters = new DynamicParameters();
    parameters.Add("@AccountId", accountId);
    parameters.Add("@StartDate", startDate);
    parameters.Add("@EndDate", endDate);
    parameters.Add("@PageSize", pageSize);
    parameters.Add("@Offset", (page - 1) * pageSize);
    
    var whereClause = "WHERE t.AccountId = @AccountId AND t.TradeDate BETWEEN @StartDate AND @EndDate";
    
    if (!string.IsNullOrEmpty(assetClass))
    {
        whereClause += " AND i.AssetClass = @AssetClass";
        parameters.Add("@AssetClass", assetClass);
    }
    
    // Using a single query with windowing function to get both total count and paged results
    var sql = $@"
        WITH TradeData AS (
            SELECT 
                t.TradeId,
                i.Name AS InstrumentName,
                t.Quantity,
                t.Price,
                t.TradeDate,
                v.Name AS ExecutionVenue,
                i.AssetClass,
                t.Direction,
                t.Quantity * t.Price * i.ContractMultiplier AS NotionalValue,
                COUNT(*) OVER() AS TotalCount
            FROM Trades t
            INNER JOIN Instruments i ON t.InstrumentId = i.InstrumentId
            INNER JOIN ExecutionVenues v ON t.ExecutionVenueId = v.VenueId
            {whereClause}
            ORDER BY t.TradeDate DESC
            OFFSET @Offset ROWS
            FETCH NEXT @PageSize ROWS ONLY
        )
        SELECT * FROM TradeData";
    
    using var connection = new SqlConnection(_connectionString);
    var trades = await connection.QueryAsync<TradeDto>(sql, parameters);
    
    var tradesList = trades.ToList();
    var totalItems = tradesList.Any() ? tradesList.First().TotalCount : 0;
    
    // Clean up the TotalCount property as it's not part of our DTO
    foreach (var trade in tradesList)
    {
        trade.TotalCount = 0;
    }
    
    return new PagedResult<TradeDto>
    {
        Items = tradesList,
        TotalItems = totalItems,
        Page = page,
        PageSize = pageSize
    };
}

What’s Different?

The raw SQL version:

  1. Uses a single query with SQL windowing functions to fetch both the total count and the data, eliminating the separate COUNT query
  2. Joins only the necessary tables with explicit control over the join conditions
  3. Pushes pagination to the database using OFFSET/FETCH NEXT instead of Skip/Take
  4. Calculates derived values at the database level (NotionalValue)
  5. Uses parameter binding for security against SQL injection

Results: The Performance Impact

The performance improvements were dramatic:

Metric Entity Framework Raw SQL Improvement Avg Response Time 98ms 47ms 52% faster Peak Response Time 153ms 72ms 53% faster Memory Allocation ~5.2MB per request ~2.1MB per request 60% reduction CPU Usage 32% 18% 44% reduction

Under high load (simulated with 1,000 concurrent users), the differences were even more pronounced:

![Performance Comparison Graph]

Not only was the endpoint faster, but the reduced resource consumption meant our servers could handle approximately 2.2x more concurrent users before performance degradation.

The real win was user satisfaction. Our most active traders immediately noticed the improved responsiveness, with one commenting: “The app feels significantly snappier, especially when I’m analyzing past trades during volatile market conditions.”

When to Consider This Approach

The decision to move away from Entity Framework shouldn’t be taken lightly. Here’s a framework to help you decide if this approach is right for your application:

Consider Raw SQL When:

  • Performance is critical to your domain: In fintech, e-commerce checkout flows, real-time bidding systems, etc.
  • You have complex queries that Entity Framework struggles to optimize
  • You’re dealing with high concurrency and need to minimize resource usage
  • You have complete control over your database schema and can optimize it accordingly
  • Your team has strong SQL expertise and can maintain hand-written queries
  • You’re performing large-scale data analysis or reporting directly from the database

Stick with Entity Framework When:

  • Development speed is more important than performance
  • Your database interactions are primarily simple CRUD operations
  • Your team is more comfortable with LINQ than SQL
  • Your application needs to support multiple database providers
  • You benefit from automatic change tracking and identity resolution

Warning signs that might indicate it’s time to optimize your data access layer include:

  • Queries consistently taking more than 50ms to execute
  • High memory pressure during peak usage
  • Database CPU utilization consistently above 70%
  • Increasing response times as your data volume grows

Best Practices for Raw SQL in .NET 10

If you decide to go the raw SQL route, here are some best practices to ensure your implementation is secure, maintainable, and performant:

1. Secure Against SQL Injection

Always use parameterized queries. Both ADO.NET and Dapper make this easy:

// DON'T do this
var sql = $"SELECT * FROM Users WHERE Username = '{username}'";
// DO this
var sql = "SELECT * FROM Users WHERE Username = @Username";
var parameters = new { Username = username };

2. Structure Your Data Access Layer

Create a clean abstraction that makes raw SQL implementation details invisible to the rest of your application:

public interface ITradeRepository
{
    Task<PagedResult<TradeDto>> GetTradeHistoryAsync(
        int accountId, 
        DateTime startDate, 
        DateTime endDate, 
        string assetClass = null, 
        int page = 1, 
        int pageSize = 20);
}
// Implementation can use raw SQL, but the interface is the same

3. Use Transactions Appropriately

Ensure data consistency for multi-operation processes:

using var connection = new SqlConnection(_connectionString);
await connection.OpenAsync();
using var transaction = connection.BeginTransaction();
try
{
    // Execute multiple commands within the transaction
    await connection.ExecuteAsync(sql1, parameters1, transaction);
    await connection.ExecuteAsync(sql2, parameters2, transaction);
    
    transaction.Commit();
}
catch
{
    transaction.Rollback();
    throw;
}

4. Cache Compiled Queries

For frequently executed queries, cache the command preparation:

// Using Dapper's CommandDefinition for caching
private static readonly CommandDefinition _tradeHistoryCommand = 
    new CommandDefinition(TradeHistorySql, commandType: CommandType.Text);
// Then in your method
var result = await connection.QueryAsync<TradeDto>(
    _tradeHistoryCommand.CommandText, 
    parameters);

5. Consider Using Micro-ORMs

Libraries like Dapper provide a middle ground — raw SQL with convenient object mapping:

var trades = await connection.QueryAsync<TradeDto>(sql, parameters);

6. Document Your SQL

Complex queries should be well-documented with comments explaining the purpose and expected performance characteristics:

-- This query fetches trade history with pagination and filtering
-- It uses a windowing function to get total count in a single query
-- Expected performance: O(log n) due to index on TradeDate
WITH TradeData AS (
    ...
)

7. Test Thoroughly

Create comprehensive tests for your data access layer:

  • Unit tests with in-memory databases for logic
  • Integration tests against real databases for performance
  • Load tests to verify behavior under concurrency

Conclusion: The Right Tool for the Right Job

Moving from Entity Framework to raw SQL in our fintech application wasn’t a condemnation of Entity Framework — it was a recognition that different scenarios call for different tools.

The migration reduced our endpoint response times by half, significantly improved resource utilization, and enhanced the user experience. For performance-critical sections of our application, the trade-off between development convenience and runtime performance was well worth it.

With .NET 10’s performance improvements, the raw SQL approach has become even more compelling for performance-sensitive applications. The runtime optimizations have reduced much of the boilerplate overhead traditionally associated with ADO.NET, making it a serious contender for data-intensive applications.

However, we still use Entity Framework for admin panels, reporting tools, and other areas where development speed trumps absolute performance. In software engineering, there are rarely universal solutions — only trade-offs.

If you’re building performance-critical applications on .NET 10, I encourage you to benchmark your own scenarios and see if this approach could benefit your projects. The results might surprise you.
